Anchored Exposures, Competing Risks, and Impossible Statistics: Mental Health–Hepatocellular Carcinoma in Veterans
Treat-to-Target in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Promise, Perils, and the Path Forward
abstract: Treat-to-target has become the organizing framework for contemporary inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) management, yet its evidence base is less robust than its widespread endorsement might suggest. The approach rests on 2 equally essential pillars: defining the right therapeutic target and adjusting treatment iteratively until that target is achieved. Over the past decade, the first pillar has advanced substantially: targets have deepened from symptomatic remission through endoscopic and histologic healing toward transmural and emerging molecular end points, supported largely by association data linking deeper remission to better long-term outcomes. The second pillar has received considerably less scrutiny. Completed randomized trials of iterative treatment adjustment have yielded mixed results in unselected populations, real-world monitoring remains inconsistent, and the most clinically pressing question, whether asymptomatic patients with residual inflammation benefit from optimizing or switching advanced therapies, remains unanswered. In this review, we critically examine both pillars: the evolution and evidence base for treatment targets in IBD, the ability of current therapies to achieve them, the lessons from pivotal treat-to-target trials, and the barriers to real-world implementation. We propose a framework for individualizing treat-to-target decisions based on disease history, inflammatory trajectory, therapeutic options, and patient preferences. Ongoing trials including QUOTIENT, VERDICT, and VECTORS may define whether the second pillar can be placed on as firm a footing as the first.

title: Referent Choice and Dose–Response Modeling Behind Moderate, Unsweetened Coffee
Accelerated Biological Aging and Risk of Early-Onset Colorectal Cancer: Findings From a Large Prospective East Asian Cohort
abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: The global increase in young-onset colorectal cancer (diagnosed before age 50) necessitates improved risk stratification. Biological age, which better reflects physiological deterioration than chronological age, may serve as a crucial indicator of disease susceptibility. We examined the association between accelerated biological aging and early-onset colorectal adenocarcinoma (EOCRC-AC) risk. METHODS: In a prospective cohort of 198,491 Korean adults under 50 years of chronological age, we estimated biological age using phenotypic age, derived from 9 routine blood biomarkers, with acceleration calculated as the residual from regressing biological age on chronological age. Cox proportional hazards models, adjusted for demographic, behavioral, and clinical factors, examined the association between biological age acceleration and incident EOCRC-AC, with colorectal neuroendocrine tumors (EOCRC-NET) analyzed as a comparator outcome. RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 7.7 years, 127 incident EOCRC-ACs and 142 EOCRC-NETs were identified through linkage with the National Cancer Registry. Individuals with biological age greater than chronological age (accelerated biological aging) had a 93% higher risk of EOCRC-ACs (hazard ratio, 1.93; 95% confidence interval, 1.28-2.91), with particularly strong associations for colon adenocarcinoma (hazard ratio, 2.32; 95% confidence interval, 1.38-3.89). Associations remained consistent across subgroups including adults younger than 45 years and lag-time sensitivity analyses. In contrast, no consistent association was observed for EOCRC-NETs. CONCLUSIONS: Accelerated biological aging is independently associated with increased EOCRC-AC risk. Biological aging measures could complement chronological age-based criteria, improving risk stratification and identifying younger individuals who may benefit from earlier or tailored screening strategies.

title: Reply
Induction of Mucosal Healing by Biologics Is Topographically Comparable in Proximal and Distal Small Bowel Crohn’s Disease
abstract: Background & aims Proximal small bowel (SB) involvement is associated with worse outcomes in Crohn's disease. We aimed to compare biologic response between the proximal and distal SB segments using video capsule endoscopy to assess the small intestinal topography of inflammation. Methods Pooled analysis of 3 prospective cohorts including patients initiating or undergoing optimization of biologic therapy, who were evaluated with SB video capsule endoscopy at baseline, end of induction (14-26 weeks), and 1 year. Mucosal inflammation was defined as Lewis score ≥135. The first 2 SB tertiles were classified as proximal SB and the third as distal SB. Proximal inflammation was defined by involvement of either of the 2 proximal tertiles. Generalized estimating equations accounted for within-patient correlation, adjusting for segment, timepoint, biologic class, and disease phenotype. Results Ninety-nine patients received biologics (53: anti-tumor necrosis factor; 43: vedolizumab; and 3: ustekinumab). Eighty-two completed end of induction, and 59 completed 1-year assessments. The rate of proximal SB inflammation decreased from 63% at baseline to 44% at the end of induction (P = .001) and 41% at 1 year (P = .003), whereas distal inflammation declined from 95% to 78% (P = .001) and 71% (P Conclusions Biologic therapy is associated with topographically comparable improvement in mucosal inflammation across proximal and distal SB segments.

title: Comparative Effectiveness of Biofeedback vs Dextranomer–Hyaluronate Injection for Fecal Incontinence: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: Background & aims Anal dextranomer injection and anorectal biofeedback therapy have not been rigorously compared in patients with fecal incontinence (FI) that is refractory to medical and behavioral therapy (MBT). This study compared their effectiveness, safety, and costs. Methods The Fecal Incontinence Treatment (FIT) study was a clinical trial conducted at 5 United States medical centers. Adults with MBT-unresponsive FI (≥4 episodes per 2 weeks) were randomized to receive either injections or biofeedback. The 3 outcomes were a ≥75% reduction in FI episodes at 3 months vs baseline; the proportion of patients with pelvic pain (grade ≥II), treatment-site infection, or serious adverse events (AEs) requiring hospitalization within 3 months of randomization; and treatment cost. Results Of 8705 screened participants, 275 began MBT and 267 completed it. Among MBT nonresponders, 200 patients (176 [88%] women, 34 [12%] men) were randomized to injections (n = 101) or biofeedback (n = 99). After 3 months, FI frequency decreased by ≥75% for similar proportions of each treatment arm (injection, n = 28/101 [27.7%] vs biofeedback, n = 29/99 [29.3%]; adjusted odds ratio, 0.9; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.5-1.7; P = .79). Seven participants (injection, n = 5; biofeedback, n = 2; P = .27) had 11 relevant AEs, of which 5 were serious, nontreatment-related AEs (injection, n = 3; biofeedback, n = 2). Compared with biofeedback, injections cost an average of $1563 (95% CI, $1477-$1649) more per patient for payers (P Conclusions In this superiority trial, neither biofeedback nor dextranomer was superior for the primary efficacy endpoint in patients with moderate-to-severe, MBT-refractory FI. Biofeedback is less expensive for payers and society. Clinicaltrials gov, Number: NCT03811821.

title: Associations of Renin–Angiotensin System Inhibitors and Calcium Channel Blockers With Liver Stiffness Dynamics and Long-Term Liver-Related Events in Metabolic Dysfunction–Associated Steatotic Liver Disease
abstract: Background & aims Hypertension is common in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), but the effects of specific antihypertensive drug classes on liver stiffness and liver-related events (LREs) remain unclear. We evaluated associations of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (RASis) and calcium channel blockers (CCBs) with changes in liver stiffness and with long-term LRE risk. Methods We analyzed data from the VCTE-Prognosis cohort, an international multicenter study with serial liver stiffness measurements. Outcomes included liver stiffness progression (≥20% increase and Baveno category upshift), liver stiffness regression (≥20% decrease and Baveno category downshift), and incident LREs. We assessed associations between baseline antihypertensive therapy and liver outcomes using Cox proportional hazards models with inverse probability of treatment weighting, comparing RASi users vs nonusers and CCB users vs nonusers. Results We followed 4302 individuals with MASLD and hypertension for a median of 4.6 years, of whom 41.2% received RASis and 32.0% received CCBs. RASi use was associated with a higher likelihood of liver stiffness regression (hazard ratio [HR], 1.220; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.010-1.474; P = .039) and associated with a lower risk of long-term LREs (HR, 0.431; 95% CI 0.261-0.714; P = .001), with no significant effect on liver stiffness progression. Conversely, CCB use was associated with a lower risk of liver stiffness progression (HR, 0.681; 95% CI, 0.521-0.890; P = .005) and LREs (HR, 0.559; 95% CI, 0.326-0.958; P = .034), but not with liver stiffness regression. Findings were consistent across subgroup and sensitivity analyses. Conclusions RASi and CCB use were associated with favorable liver stiffness trajectories and lower risk of long-term LREs in individuals with MASLD and hypertension.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Advanced Therapies as Induction Therapy for Ulcerative Colitis: An Updated Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background & aims Advanced therapies (ATs) are central to the management of moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (UC). The expanding therapeutic landscape and limited head-to-head trials necessitate updated comparative effectiveness analyses. We performed a systematic review and network meta-analysis to assess the efficacy and safety of ATs as induction therapy for UC. Methods We searched MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL. We included phase 3 randomized controlled trials evaluating approved ATs or agents in late-stage development for induction therapy in moderate-to-severe UC. Pairwise meta-analyses and network meta-analyses were conducted using a frequentist random-effects model. Confidence was evaluated using the Confidence in the Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework. The primary outcome was clinical remission; secondary outcomes included endoscopic improvement, serious adverse events, adverse events leading to discontinuation, and serious infections. Analyses were stratified by prior exposure to ATs. Results Thirty-three induction trials involving 17 therapies were included. Upadacitinib demonstrated the highest relative efficacy for clinical remission (risk ratio, 6.90; 95% confidence interval, 3.54-12.45; P score, 0.95; high confidence) and endoscopic improvement (risk ratio, 5.29; 95% confidence interval, 3.38-8.28; P score, 0.97; moderate confidence). In AT-naïve patients, obefazimod and upadacitinib showed the highest efficacy, whereas in AT-experienced patients, upadacitinib, ustekinumab, and tofacitinib ranked highest. Anti-p19 inhibitors, including risankizumab, subcutaneous guselkumab, and mirikizumab, were associated with the most favorable safety profiles for serious adverse events and adverse events leading to discontinuation, although confidence in safety estimates was lower. Conclusions Upadacitinib has high efficacy for induction of clinical remission and endoscopic improvement in AT-naïve and AT-experienced patients. Novel therapies, like obefazimod and subcutaneous guselkumab, may represent highly effective alternatives. Anti-p19 inhibitors offer a favorable safety profile. Registration PROSPERO, Number: CRD42024547849.

title: Real-Time Abdominal Pain–Daily Life Trigger Associations in Irritable Bowel Syndrome: A Multicenter Experience Sampling Method Study
abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: Gastrointestinal symptoms in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) are influenced by daily life triggers. This study examined real-time associations of abdominal pain with psychosocial and environmental triggers utilizing an Experience Sampling Method (ESM)-based patient reported outcome measure, while considering the moderating effects of IBS severity and comorbidities. METHODS: This prospective multicenter study included 360 patients with Rome IV IBS (81% female; mean age, 40.5 years) from 7 European countries. Participants completed a 7-day ESM with 10 random daily questionnaires on abdominal pain and potential triggers. Linear mixed-effects models analyzed univariable and multivariable associations between pain and triggers, concurrently and predictively (time-lagged), accounting for severity (Irritable Bowel Syndrome Severity Scoring System), mental (Patient Health Questionnaire-9, Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7), and somatic (Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory, Patient Health Questionnaire-15) scores. RESULTS: Significant bidirectional associations were observed between abdominal pain and daily life triggers. Higher positive affect and environmental comfort were associated with lower pain (b = -0.23; P < .001 and b = -0.18; P < .01), whereas negative affect and eating were associated with higher pain (b = 0.34 and b = 0.13; both P < .001). The associations were consistent across patients, some of which were moderated by IBS and/or comorbid symptom severity (P < .05). Predictive associations were less frequent and weaker (b = -0.03 to 0.07; P < .05). Few significant associations persisted in multivariable analyses. CONCLUSIONS: This international ESM study provides real-time insight into the dynamic interplay between abdominal pain and daily life triggers in IBS. Concurrent and weaker predictive associations highlight the temporal complexity of symptom-trigger dynamics, whereas multivariable findings suggest that daily life factors are inter-related rather than isolated triggers. Variation by IBS and comorbid symptom severity underscores the individualized nature of symptom patterns and supports personalized care in IBS. CLINICALTRIALS: gov, Number: NCT02880722 (study 2, impending for study 1).

title: Avoidant/restrictive food intake across the gastrointestinal tract
abstract: Background Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) is characterized by reduced dietary intake leading to medical and/or psychosocial impairment, independent of body image concerns. We aim to assess ARFID screening and characteristics in patients with gastrointestinal disorders versus healthy volunteers (HV), and its associations with symptom severity, extraintestinal symptoms and depression scores. Methods We analyzed 92 HV and 467 patients from seven tertiary cohorts: irritable bowel syndrome (IBS, n=88), functional dyspepsia (FD, n=83), constipation (n=59), reflux (n=107), globus (n=45), dysphagia (n=37), and achalasia (n=48), grouped into non-esophageal (IBS, FD, constipation) and esophageal disorders (reflux, globus, dysphagia and achalasia). Assessments included Rome IV criteria, extraintestinal symptoms and depression scores (PHQ-12/9), and ARFID screening. ARFID+ was defined as NIAS+ (≥1 subscale cutoff: picky eating ≥10, appetite ≥9, fear ≥10) plus DSM-5 impairment. Odds ratios were derived from multiple logistic regression with three-level hierarchical approach adjusted for symptom severity, extra-intestinal, and depression symptoms. Results Compared to HV, IBS (OR=15.0), FD (OR=10.6), constipation (OR=18.2), reflux (OR=5.2) and dysphagia (OR=7.0) were associated with ARFID+, whereas globus or achalasia were not. A higher prevalence of ARFID+ was observed in non-esophageal versus esophageal disorders (24% vs. 11%; OR=2.7, p Conclusion ARFID symptoms are more prevalent across non-esophageal disorders compared to esophageal disorders. Within non-esophageal disorders, symptoms severity and food-related abdominal pain are associated with ARFID+, and mostly characterized by fear of aversive consequences.

title: Real-world hepatic safety of the potassium-competitive acid blocker: A RUCAM-adjudicated multicenter cohort study
abstract: Background & aims Early-generation potassium-competitive acid blockers (P-CABs) were withdrawn during clinical development because of hepatotoxicity, and long-term real-world hepatic safety data for newer P-CABs remain scarce. Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) ascertainment in observational studies is further limited by the reliance on nonspecific outcome definitions. We aimed to evaluate the hepatic safety of tegoprazan compared with proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2RAs) using Roussel Uclaf Causality Assessment Method (RUCAM)-based adjudication. Methods This large-scale, multicenter retrospective cohort study used a new-user, active-comparator design including users of tegoprazan, PPIs, or H2RAs with ≥30 cumulative defined daily doses (cDDDs). Propensity score matching (PSM) balanced demographics, comorbidities, hepatotoxic co-medications, and baseline liver biochemistry. The primary outcome was RUCAM-adjudicated DILI (score ≥3); hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated by Cox regression with Firth's penalized likelihood for rare events. Results Of 363,340 screened patients, 11,190 were included; PSM yielded 5,586 (1,862/group). RUCAM-possible DILI was very rare, with 3, 2, and 3 events (0.17, 0.07, and 0.15 per 100 person-years) in the tegoprazan, PPI, and H2RA groups, respectively. No increased risk was detected for tegoprazan versus H2RAs (Firth-penalized HR 0.98; 95% CI, 0.20-4.95) or PPIs (HR 1.63; 95% CI, 0.28-9.56), with wide confidence intervals. No case exceeded the "possible" RUCAM threshold. Conclusions No increased risk of RUCAM-possible DILI was detected for tegoprazan compared with PPIs or H2RAs, although the small number of events precludes a conclusion of equivalent safety. The rarity of RUCAM-possible events across all acid-suppressive drug classes raises the possibility that previously reported signals may partly reflect differences in outcome ascertainment.

title: Weight changes differentially impact MASLD incidence, progression and outcomes based on genetic and metabolic risk profiles
abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) comprises heterogeneous subgroups with liver- vs. cardiovascular-related adverse outcomes. Weight management is crucial in MASLD prevention and treatment, but its effect on MASLD subgroups is unclear. METHODS: We assessed the impact of body weight dynamics on incident MASLD, steatosis resolution, fibrosis risk regression and related cardiovascular diseases (CVD) from the UK biobank. Genetic subgroups (i.e., hepatic and systemic) were defined by polygenic risk scores, a metabolic risk group by lipid accumulation product. A Cox proportional model evaluated impacts across the general population and sex-stratified subgroups. RESULTS: Among 11,882 participants without MASLD, 1,350 developed MASLD during a median follow-up of 4 years. Each 1% reduction in body weight was associated with a 10% lower risk of MASLD (HR = 0.90 [0.89-0.91]). Among 6,013 participants with MASLD, 753 achieved MASLD resolution; each 1% weight reduction was associated with a 9% higher rate of resolution (HR = 1.09 [1.08-1.10]). Weight loss was also associated with a lower risk of MASLD-related CVD (HR = 0.98 [0.97-0.99]). Recommended weight loss for MASLD prevention (male/female) differed across hepatic (8.7%/13.1%), systemic (8.0%/11.8%), and metabolic-risk (10.9%/14.4%) groups. Estimated lower weight-loss thresholds associated with MASLD resolution were 5.3%/13.3% in hepatic-risk, 10.2%/10.7% in systemic-risk, and 5.7%/5.8% in metabolic-risk participants (male/female). For fibrosis-risk regression, no robust threshold was identified in hepatic-risk participants, but 7.7%/5.6% in metabolic-risk participants (male/female). CONCLUSION: Individualized weight management should be recommended according to the genetic and metabolic risk profiles of individuals.

title: Late-Night Eating is Associated with MASLD and Cirrhosis: The Nurses' Health Study and Health Professionals' Follow-Up Study
Alcohol-associated liver disease
abstract: Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) is the leading cause of liver-related mortality in Western countries. The assessment of histological severity in ALD now relies predominantly on non-invasive methods, particularly elastography and blood-based tests, commercially available or laboratory-developed. These non-invasive approaches have largely replaced the need for liver biopsy. Management of ALD is based primarily on the treatment of alcohol use disorder, and access to pharmacological therapies and addiction specialists should be improved. At present, there is no specific treatment for ALD, with the exception of corticosteroid therapy for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH), a distinct clinical entity associated with a poor prognosis that requires specialized management. In patients with advanced ALD who fail to improve despite sustained alcohol abstinence, liver transplantation remains the only effective therapeutic option. In this setting, a dedicated and multidisciplinary care pathway should be established to optimize patient selection, management, and long-term outcomes.

title: Diffuse esophageal eosinophilia is associated with increased endoscopic severity and topical steroid non-response in patients with eosinophilic esophagitis
abstract: Background and aims Variability of esophageal eosinophil distributions and its impact on disease presentation and treatment outcomes in eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is unclear. We aimed to determine whether isolated proximal or distal involvement differs from diffuse involvement in EoE presentation and treatment outcomes. Methods This retrospective cohort study analyzed patients of all ages with newly diagnosed EoE from the UNC EoE Clinicopathologic database. Patients were classified as distal esophagus-only (≥15 eos/hpf), proximal-only (≥15 eos/hpf), and diffuse involvement (≥15 eos/hpf in both regions). Outcomes included histologic response ( Results Of 888 cases of EoE, eosinophil counts were higher in the distal (54.8±44.7) versus proximal esophagus (44.0±40.1; p Conclusions EoE patients with diffuse esophageal eosinophilic involvement had greater baseline disease severity and decreased histologic and endoscopic treatment response to topical corticosteroids than those with localized disease. Diffuse disease involvement could be an important marker for risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making in EoE disease management.

title: Early-life animal exposure was not associated with risk of inflammatory bowel disease: a nationwide birth cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) continues to rise globally. Early-life environmental exposures may influence immune development, but evidence regarding animal exposure remains inconsistent. We examined whether early-life exposure to pets or farm animals was associated with offspring risk of IBD in a prospective birth cohort. METHODS: In this nationwide cohort study based on the Danish National Birth Cohort, prenatal offspring exposure to pets or farm animals, based on maternal reports, was used as the primary indicator of early-life animal exposure. Early-childhood exposure from birth to 18 months was examined in exposure-window analyses. Incident IBD, Crohn's disease (CD), and ulcerative colitis (UC) were identified through national registries. Associations were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models. RESULTS: Among 90,306 offspring, 46% were prenatally exposed to pets and 7% to farm animals. During median follow-up of 24 years, 615 offspring developed IBD. Pet exposure was not associated with IBD risk (aHR 1.05, 95% CI 0.89-1.24), nor was farm animal exposure (aHR 1.00, 95% CI 0.73-1.37). Findings were consistent across specific animal categories and in analyses of CD and UC separately. In exposure-window analyses restricted to 63,958 offspring with maternal reports of both pre- and postnatal exposure, no associations were observed among offspring exposed only during pregnancy (aHR 1.10, 95% CI 0.75-1.63) or only during early childhood (aHR 0.73, 95% CI 0.46-1.15). CONCLUSIONS: Early-life exposure to pets or farm animals was not associated with offspring risk of IBD. These findings suggest that early-life animal exposure may not be a major determinant of disease development.

title: Optimal Incidence Threshold for Cost-Effective Hepatocellular Carcinoma Surveillance in Alcohol-Associated Cirrhosis
abstract: Background & aims Current guidelines recommend routine hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) surveillance in patients with cirrhosis when annual HCC incidence exceeds 1 per 100 person-years, a threshold derived from older studies and not specific to alcohol-associated cirrhosis. However, contemporary data suggest that HCC incidence in this population is often below 1%, leaving the value of routine surveillance uncertain. Methods We developed a Markov-based state-transition microsimulation model to simulate the natural history of HCC and subsequent treatment pathways in patients with alcohol-associated cirrhosis in the setting of the United States. The model compared biannual surveillance with ultrasound and alpha fetoprotein vs no surveillance separately for 2 distinct cohorts: patients who continued to actively consume alcohol and patients who had achieved sustained abstinence. Inputs included the natural history of alcohol-associated cirrhosis, HCC incidence, test performance, surveillance adherence, and contemporary treatment. Sensitivity analyses examined the robustness of model assumptions and findings. Results Biannual surveillance becomes cost-effective when annual HCC incidence reached approximately 0.45 per 100 person-years using a willingness-to-pay threshold of $100,000 per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among active drinkers, surveillance yielded an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of $18,952 per QALY; among abstinent patients, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was $56,000 per QALY. Per 100,000 patients, routine surveillance generated an estimated 2083 additional life-years and 992 QALYs in active drinkers and 3357 life-years and 1700 QALYs in abstinent patients. Conclusions Routine biannual HCC surveillance with ultrasound and alpha fetoprotein is cost-effective for patients with alcohol-associated cirrhosis in the United States when HCC incidence exceeds 0.45 per 100 person-years, substantially below the historically cited 1 per 100 person-years threshold. Updating clinical guidelines to reflect these contemporary thresholds could improve early HCC detection in this high-risk population.

EsoEinstein: A Multimodal AI System Integrating EGD and FLIP for Esophageal Motility Assessment
abstract: Background & aims Achalasia diagnosis relies on integrating endoscopic, functional, and physiologic testing, yet high-resolution manometry (HRM) is invasive, uncomfortable, and resource limited. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a potential pathway to streamline this workflow. This study aimed to develop and validate AI models for diagnosing achalasia using esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD), Functional Lumen Imaging Probe (FLIP) panometry, and their combined multimodal integration, using Chicago Classification v4.0 (CCv4.0) as the reference standard. Methods In this retrospective study, 1,802 adult patients who underwent HRM and had available EGD and/or FLIP data at a tertiary center were included. Separate deep learning models were trained for EGD videos, FLIP heatmap images, and a multimodal transformer that integrated both modalities. Primary outcomes were sensitivity, specificity, and AUC for detecting achalasia. Results The 1,802-patient cohort was partitioned into training (n=1,522), validation (n=212), and test sets (n=68) for model development and evaluation. For the test set, the EGD model achieved sensitivity 0.724, specificity 0.974, and AUC 0.908. FLIP achieved sensitivity 0.862, specificity 0.821, and AUC 0.931. The multimodal model performed the best, with sensitivity 0.931, specificity 0.846, and AUC 0.969. Cochran's Q test found no statistically significant differences across models. Conclusion Multimodal AI that integrates endoscopic and FLIP data achieves expert-level accuracy and has potential as a less invasive approach for diagnosing achalasia. To realize this potential, future work must validate the system in real-world settings to evaluate its impact on diagnostic timelines and longitudinal patient outcomes.

Personalized Prehabilitation: A Pathway to Improved Frailty Metrics and Survival in Liver Transplant Candidates
abstract: Background & aims Outpatient prehabilitation can potentially improve frailty in liver transplant (LT) candidates. Our aim was to determine the impact of prehabilitation on physical fitness and mortality, and to identify the minimum clinically important change needed to improve survival. Methods In this ambispective cohort study, LT candidates underwent baseline evaluation with a dedicated physical therapist (PT) and were prescribed a personalized prehabilitation program based on their functional status. Liver frailty index (LFI), 6-min walk test (6MWT), and gait speed test (GST) were assessed. Multilevel linear mixed-effects models and multivariable survival analyses were fitted, including competing risks models against LT. Results A total of 1275 patients (59% male, age 57±11, MELD 14±6) attended 1973 LT-PT visits. Of these, 355 attended two or more follow-up visits, participating in the prehabilitation program. At baseline, median LFI was 3.8 (3.2-4.4), 6MWT 336 m (243-403), and GST 1 (0.8-1.2); 23%, 26%, and 29% of the cohort were frail by each tool, respectively. Among subjects who improved LFI (n=226/352), the absolute change was -0.39 (-0.32 to -0.46), and for 6MWT (n=212/334) it was 54 m (43-64); fewer than half improved GST. A total of 667 (55%) patients were waitlisted, 462 (37%) transplanted, and 335 (26%) died. LFI improvement by at least 0.4 was associated with a ∼50% reduction in mortality (HR=0.56, p=0.037). Improvement in 6MWT was not associated with a survival advantage. Conclusion Individualized prehabilitation in LT candidates was associated with significant improvement in LFI and 6MWT. A minimum LFI improvement of 0.4 was associated with improved survival and could be considered a minimal clinically important difference for frailty interventions in LT candidates.

title: Redefining Cholangiocarcinoma Management: Breakthroughs and Their Clinical Implications for Clinical Practice
abstract: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is a heterogeneous group of malignancies that originates in the biliary epithelium and is anatomically classified into intrahepatic (iCCA) and extrahepatic (eCCA) subtypes. These tumors often progress silently and are associated with a poor prognosis, limiting the opportunities for timely intervention. Most patients do not have identifiable risk factors. Recent improvements in imaging techniques and next-generation sequencing (NGS) have enhanced diagnostic accuracy and enabled identification of actionable molecular alterations (e.g., FGFR2 fusions, IDH1 mutations). These advances have supported biomarker-driven therapies and integration of immunotherapy into first-line treatment. However, persistent gaps in risk stratification and early detection remain major barriers to improving outcomes. This review highlights recent advancements in CCA treatment and management, emphasizing practical considerations for gastroenterologists and hepatologists.

General Population Screening For Celiac Disease: A Scoping Review of Evidence, Outcomes, and Implementation
abstract: Background and aims Early diagnosis of celiac disease (CeD) through general population screening remains controversial. This review summarizes the remaining evidence gaps limiting implementation of population-based screening for CeD. Methods A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR. PubMed was searched for literature related to CeD-screening published up to April 18, 2025. Twelve paired reviewers independently screened selected abstracts and assessed full texts. Included articles were then categorized by primary outcome and summarized descriptively. Results Of 2,014 abstracts, 172 full-text articles were included with 12 identified outside of the search. Population-based studies indicate that CeD is common yet markedly underdiagnosed, with screening identifying 60-75% of cases not detected by routine clinical practice. Most affected individuals lack clinical features or known affected family members, highlighting the limitation of symptom-driven and targeted screening strategies. Screening-identified individuals benefit from earlier diagnosis with improved health outcomes and quality of life, at the risk of decreased dietary adherence and reduced social functioning. Case-finding, targeted screening, and population-based screening each offer different trade-offs with respect to acceptability, cost, and detection rates. Health economic analyses demonstrate that both case-finding and general population screening can be cost effective, although the magnitude is impacted by diagnostic delay and associated modeled complications. Conclusions Current evidence supports potential value of general population screening for CeD. Concerns for health system capacity, cost and management of individuals identified through screening continue to limit consideration of population-based screening for CeD. Implementation studies evaluating real-world outcomes from screening, are essential to address these evidence gaps.

title: Efficacy and Safety of Guselkumab in Patients with Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis: A Prospective Real-World Study
abstract: Background and aims Guselkumab (GUS), selective IL-23p19 inhibitor that also binds to CD64+ cells, is approved for the treatment of moderately-to-severely active Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Real-world evidence of effectiveness and safety is needed. Methods We prospectively enrolled adult patients with IBD initiating GUS at our tertiary center between 9/2024 and 1/2026. Patients were followed for up to 52 weeks. Clinical and biochemical data were collected at designated time points on patients' activity indices and adverse events (AEs). Clinical remission was defined as a Harvey-Bradshaw Index (HBI) Results We followed 234 patients who initiated GUS (142 CD, 92 UC). Week 12 clinical remission was achieved in 76.8% of patients with CD (HBI Conclusion In this large real-world prospective experience of GUS for IBD, we describe high rates of remission and an overall safety profile that is similar to that seen in the pivotal trials.

High burden of potentially undiagnosed MASH in a general population in Sweden
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Few studies have explored the prevalence and outcomes of fibrotic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in the general population. We aimed to characterize patients at risk of MASH using the validated Fibrotic NASH Index (FNI) and to compare the incidence of major adverse liver outcomes (MALO), major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and mortality between FNI risk groups and patients with established MASH. METHODS: Patients were classified as high risk (FNI≥0.33 and ≥ 1 cardiometabolic risk factor), or low-risk (FNI<0.1 +/- cardiometabolic risk factors) using laboratory data from routine clinical care in Stockholm, Sweden in 2010-2020. Patients with established MASH had a recorded ICD-10 code (K75.8) in Swedish specialist care (1998-2022). Data were analysed using Cox regression models and MALO, MACE and mortality were measured in number of events, cumulative incidence, and incidence rates. RESULTS: FNI was available in 162,456 patients, of which 23% were considered at high risk of MASH, and 39% considered low-risk. Among patients with established MASH (n=615), MALO's were more common than in high-risk FNI patients (45% vs 0.6%) at baseline. The rate of incident MALO was higher in diagnosed MASH patients vs the high-risk FNI group (adjusted HR [aHR]=6.73, 95%CI=4.03-11.23) and higher in high vs low-risk FNI group (aHR=4.6, 95%CI=3.9-5.4). The rate of MACE was also higher in high- vs low-risk (aHR=1.8, 95%CI=1.7-1.8) but not significantly different in high-risk vs diagnosed patients (aHR=0.6, 95%CI=0.3-1.2). CONCLUSION: There is a large burden of potentially undiagnosed at-risk MASH in patients from a general population with risk factors for MASH. Almost half of patients with established MASH already have MALO at baseline, reinforcing the need for earlier diagnosis.

title: Prevalence and outcomes of acute presentations of autoimmune hepatitis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: Background and aims Acute presentations of autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) ranging from acute hepatitis to acute liver failure (ALF) and acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) are diagnostically challenging and clinically heterogeneous. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the prevalence of acute AIH presentations and to evaluate transplant-free survival (TFS) across subtypes. Methods We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library from inception through July 2025 for observational studies reporting acute AIH presentations. Random-effects models generated pooled prevalence and TFS estimates, with a general/unselected-cohort sensitivity analysis performed where feasible. Study quality was assessed using the JBI checklist. Results Across 10 studies reporting both a total AIH cohort size and a separately quantified acute presentation, the pooled proportion of AIH patients presenting acutely was 39% (95% CI 27%-54.0%; I 2 =95%). Thirty-four studies were included to describe different acute phenotypes. The pooled prevalence of acute non-severe AIH (ANS-AIH), acute severe AIH (AS-AIH), AIH-associated ALF, acute/severe exacerbation of chronic AIH, and AIH-associated ACLF was 21% (95% CI, 14%-30%; I 2 =75.6%), 15.0% (95% CI, 9%-23%; I 2 =79.4%), 3% (95% CI, 1%-9%; I 2 =90.1%), 15% (95% CI, 9%-25%; I 2 =91.8%), and 11% (95% CI, 7%-16%; I 2 =78.5%), respectively. TFS was standardized to 90-day timepoint where feasible. Pooled 90-day TFS was 79% (95% CI 36-96%; I 2 =0%) for AS-AIH and 19% (11%-31%; I 2 =0%) for AIH-ALF. Heterogeneity remained substantial across most phenotypes. Conclusions Acute presentations are common in AIH and span phenotypes with profoundly different clinical trajectories. While most patients with ANS-AIH, acute/severe exacerbations and AS-AIH achieve favorable outcomes with timely therapy, progression to ALF carries poor TFS.

title: Intravenous Versus Subcutaneous Induction with Guselkumab: Week 12 and Week 96 Efficacy in GALAXI 2 & 3 and GRAVITI
abstract: Background & aims Guselkumab is approved for intravenous (IV) or subcutaneous (SC) induction in moderately to severely active Crohn's disease (CD). We compared outcomes and evaluated the onset of guselkumab efficacy with IV or SC induction and charted the long-term efficacy and safety of guselkumab SC maintenance following either route of induction. Methods Treatment effects of IV and SC induction were compared via inverse probability weighting (IPW) analysis. Clinical, endoscopic, and inflammatory biomarker outcomes in participants randomized to placebo or guselkumab in GALAXI (IV induction) and GRAVITI (SC induction) were evaluated through Week 12, including analyses across predefined subgroups. Efficacy and safety outcomes through Week 96 were reported from the long-term extensions (LTEs) of GALAXI and GRAVITI. Results IPW analysis found no statistical differences (all P > .05) between guselkumab IV and SC induction efficacy. In the per-trial comparisons with placebo, both IV and SC induction were statistically superior for Week 12 clinical response (Δ 34.5-42.8); similar efficacy was seen in Week 12 analyses of clinical remission rates (Δ 25.1-34.9), and abdominal pain (Δ 0.6-0.7) and stool frequency scores (Δ 1.2-2.0). Both routes of guselkumab induction provided rapid onset of efficacy, with clinical response and clinical remission observed by Week 4. IV and SC guselkumab induction regimens were similarly effective at Week 12 across prespecified subgroups of baseline disease location and clinical, endoscopic, and inflammatory biomarker disease activity. Adverse events during induction with SC and IV guselkumab were similar and comparable to placebo. Efficacy was maintained after 96 weeks of guselkumab therapy: long-term outcomes of clinical remission, endoscopic response, endoscopic remission, and deep remission were unaffected by the route of induction: 39.5-51.2% of guselkumab participants achieved deep remission at Week 96. Exposure-adjusted incidence rates of AEs, SAEs, and AEs leading to discontinuation through Week 96 were lower with guselkumab versus placebo and generally similar between GALAXI and GRAVITI. Conclusions IV and SC induction with guselkumab were equally effective across a wide range of patients with CD, including those with high baseline disease activity. Efficacy with guselkumab through Week 96 was unaffected by the route of induction. No new safety concerns were identified.

title: Real-time Voice-Guided Artificial Intelligence Improves Biliopancreatic Endosonography Quality: A Randomized Trial
abstract: Background and aims Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) quality is operator-dependent, and adherence to guideline-recommended multi-station biliopancreatic scanning remains suboptimal. We developed a device (named EUS-GUIDEQ), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based real-time EUS navigation and quality-control system providing station recognition, voice-guided prompts, and quantitative completeness feedback. We evaluated its performance and clinical utility. Methods EUS-GUIDEQ was developed from 27,072 annotated biliopancreatic EUS images obtained from 189 patients and validated on independent datasets consisting of 1,500 internal images and 2,062 multicenter external images. We then conducted a prospective, single-center, randomized controlled trial (1:1) comparing AI-assisted versus standard EUS. The primary endpoint was completeness of standardized scanning stations. Secondary endpoints included station-level and landmarks completeness, procedure duration (observation time excluding additional interventions), and adverse events. Outcomes were adjudicated by blinded expert review of recorded videos. Results Station-classification model achieved accuracies of 94.2% internally and 78.8% externally. Between December 12, 2023, and May 16, 2025, 266 patients were analyzed (AI-assisted n=132; control n=134). Overall station completeness was higher with EUS-GUIDEQ assistance (median [IQR] 1.00 [0.94-1.00] vs 0.81 [0.75-0.88]; P Conclusions In a randomized trial, voice-guided real-time AI navigation improved guideline-level biliopancreatic EUS process quality, as measured by station completeness, but increased procedure time. Multicenter, multi-vendor prospective validation is warranted.

title: Endoscopic Balloon Dilation Versus Endoscopic Stricturotomy for Short Crohn's Disease Strictures: The BEST-CD Randomized Trial
abstract: Background and aims Endoscopic balloon dilation (EBD) is the standard therapy for Crohn's disease (CD) strictures but is limited by recurrence and reinterventions. Randomized comparative data on endoscopic stricturotomy (ES) vs EBD are lacking. Methods In this randomized controlled trial, adults (18-65 years) with symptomatic CD and short ( Results Of 164 patients screened, 106 were randomised (EBD n=53; ES n=53). In the intention-to-treat population, clinical recurrence at 1 year was lower with ES than EBD (30.1% vs 54.7%; p=0·01), as were reintervention (24.5% vs 49.1%; p=0·01), emergency visits (18.9% vs 50.9%; p=0·001), and hospitalisations (15.1% vs 34%; p=0·02). Surgery did not differ significantly (1.9% vs 11.3%; p=0·11). In 12-month time-to-event analyses, EBD was associated with higher hazards of clinical recurrence (HR 2.27, 95% CI 1.23-4.18) and reintervention (HR 2.40, 95% CI 1.23-4.68), with consistent findings for emergency visits and hospitalisation. Adverse events were similar (13·2% vs 22.6%; p=0·30). Conclusion ES was associated with lower 1-year clinical recurrence and reintervention than EBD for short CD strictures. These findings support ES as a promising endoscopic strategy in expert centres and warrant validation in multicentre studies. (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT05521867).

title: Safety of Janus kinase inhibitors, ustekinumab, and anti-interleukin-23 in older patients with immune-mediated diseases
abstract: Background and aims Data on the safety of newer advanced therapies (AT) for immune-mediated inflammatory diseases (IMIDs) remain limited in older patients, and how the underlying IMID type influences treatment safety is unknown. Methods We systematically searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase for studies evaluating the safety of anti-IL12/23 and -IL23 agents, and JAKi in older patients with IMIDs, including inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and psoriasis. Eligible studies included patients who initiated therapy at age ≥50 years and reported outcomes in comparison with (1) younger patients receiving the same therapy, (2) older patients receiving non-AT, or (3) older patients receiving a different AT. Data on infections, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), venous thromboembolism (VTE), malignancy, and mortality were extracted. Pooled odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model. Results Seventy-nine studies were included. Compared to other AT, JAKi were associated with a higher risk of infections (OR 1.38; 95% CI, 1.22-1.55) and serious infections (1.27; 1.06-1.52). No increase in MACE, VTE, or malignancy risk was seen overall. Among adults > 60 years, there was an increased risk of VTE in rheumatologic cohorts (3.28; 1.16-9.27) that was absent in IBD (0.99; 0.58-1.70) (p for difference = 0.045). Compared with anti-TNF, Anti-IL-12/23 and -IL-23 agents had a lower risk of serious infections (0.76; 0.68-0.84). Conclusion In older patients with IMIDs, anti-IL-12/23 and -IL-23 agents had lower serious infection risk while JAKi had an increased risk. JAKi showed a possible disease-specific thromboembolic signal in rheumatologic but not IBD cohorts.

title: Development and validation of the OpENS model for upper gastrointestinal cancer screening across diverse regions in China
abstract: BACKGROUND & AIMS: The application and performance of upper gastrointestinal (UGI) cancer risk stratification tools across diverse regions in China remains unclear. We aimed to develop decision-making tools for personalized screening adapted to different regions. METHODS: Participants were recruited from 386 hospitals in 2023 and followed up to December 2025. Individuals with advanced neoplasias in the esophagus, cardia and non-cardiac gastric region (NCGR) confirmed during screening, and UGI cancer patients identified within a six-month period, were counted as advanced neoplasia cases. Participants were grouped into new (NP) and returning patients (RP) according to prior history of UGI endoscopy. Individual risk factors were collected and multivariate models were constructed and externally validated. A risk score was calculated using decile ranking of the model scores. Regions were categorized into high-, medium-, and low-risk based on local UGI cancer incidence. The ratio of the number needed to screen (NNS) between universal and high-risk individual screening was calculated to evaluate efficiency improvement. RESULTS: 17,688 (2.63%) UGI advanced neoplasia cases were confirmed in 673,126 participants. The AUCs of the multivariate models exceeded 0.850 for esophagus and cardia, and 0.750 for NCGR. For individual risk assessment, the optimal risk score screening threshold was 8, yielding a 2.3-fold efficiency gain. For regional screening strategies, the optimal screening threshold was 1 for NPs and 5 for RPs in high-risk regions, 3 for NPs and 6 for RPs in medium-risk regions, and 6 for NPs and 8 for RPs in low-risk regions. This yielded 1.02-, 1.19- and 2.07-fold efficiency gain in each region, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: The risk stratification model can be readily implemented and increases the efficiency of opportunistic UGI cancer screening across diverse regions in China.
